newsitem.title: USA: Union supporters rally for U.S. newspaper strikers.
newsitem.headline: Union supporters rally for U.S. newspaper strikers.

text.p: Energized by a key legal victory, about 50,000 people gathered under a muggy sky Saturday in support of striking newspaper workers for a rally and march past the offices of Detroit's two daily newspapers.
Top union leaders from around the country participated in the event, called Action Motown!, which was previously scheduled to generate support for the six striking unions.
The strikers got an unexpected boost Friday when a federal administrative law judge ruled the strike was caused by management's unfair labor practices.
"This is all about keeping the faith with working people who are fighting for the future," Teamster President Ron Carey told the crowd.
"We're here to let Gannett and Knight-Ridder -- and to let corporate America -- know we aren't giving up and we aren't going away," he said.

Gannett Co. owns the News and Knight-Ridder Inc. owns the Free Press. The papers are editorially separate but published by a joint operating company. About 2,500 editorial, distribution and production workers walked off their jobs July 13, 1995.

Lou Moye, a United Auto Worker member from St. Louis, said he was pleased to see the variety of union support at the rally. In addition to Teamsters and UAW leaders, AFL-CIO President John Sweeney also attended.
"We have to work and turn it into a wider boycott against Gannett and Knight-Ridder," Moye said.
Detroit Police Inspector John Whitty estimated there were 50,000 people in the crowd. Marchers started at Tiger Stadium and finished in Hart Plaza.

Separately, UAW vice president Richard Shoemaker said the union still hoped to reach an agreement with General Motors Corp. to end a strike by 5,800 workers at the automaker's Pontiac, Mich., full-size pickup truck plant.

The union still has several locals that do not have new national agreements with the company, some of which could erupt into strikes. Shoemaker said the union planned to send more people into the field to study those situations. But he said that might not occur until after the automaker's two-week summer shutdown, which ends in the middle of July.
